newsitem.title: USA: Brent sales shake up U.S. Gulf Coast, Latam quiet.
newsitem.headline: Brent sales shake up U.S. Gulf Coast, Latam quiet.

text.p: Sales of North Sea Brent crude into the U.S. Gulf Coast have shaken up the foreign crude scene, traders said.
Swiss-based Glencore sold two cargoes of Brent to a U.S. refiner late last week at around April West Texas Intermediate/Cushing minus 30 cents a barrel, traders said.
But a third cargo was subsequently sold for a discount of 60 cents, they said.
"They're dumping (the crude). Nobody can figure it out. It doesn't appear that they made any money off of it," one Texas trader said.
Offers are now going for a discount of 60-80 cents a barrel for April arrival, traders said.
One trader speculated that Glencore was holding a paper position to offset its physical sales.
The spread between April WTI and Brent was around $1.15-20 a barrel Monday afternoon, a narrow window that ordinarily would discourage transatlantic trade.
"Sellers aren't happy and buyers are afraid to take a decision" for fear that prices will fall further if they wait," a trader said.

West African Qua Iboe was pegged around 30-40 cents under WTI for April, but sellers seemed to be waiting for prices to fully gestate before giving birth to prices that might compete with Glencore's aggressive sales, traders said.
Latin American spot activity was quiet. A half cargo of Colombian Cano Limon loading in March was heard still available, traders said.
Mexico and Venezuela continue to price their sour crudes aggressively and flexibly in a bid to retain and expand market share in the key U.S. market, traders said.
Venezuelan Mesa-30 was assessed at a discount of $3.25 a barrel, down from $2.90 a month ago.
